query: Earlier automotive-catalyst research reported that Cu–Ni catalysts can oxidize CO and hydrocarbons at lower temperatures without platinum-group metals, while Pd–Cu and Pt–Cu catalysts can resist poisoning by H2O and NO and enable oxidation below 150 °C. Multi-principal-element catalysts in nearly equiatomic ratios have also been explored as a framework for combining high activity, thermal stability, and reduced platinum-group-metal use. These prior results demonstrate individual capabilities but do not establish the combined performance demanded by increasingly stringent regulations: clean exhaust during transient and low-temperature operation, resistance to relevant poisons, and durability over a vehicle lifetime despite the mileage-related degradation observed in real-driving-emission studies. Starting from a near-equiatomic, multi-principal-element automotive alloy catalyst, what single intervention could address this combined activity, poisoning-resistance, and lifetime-durability problem without sacrificing low platinum-group-metal use? State one hypothesis identifying the intervention, explaining how it would work, predicting the change relative to the unmodified catalyst, defining the exhaust and aging conditions over which it should apply, citing supporting prior evidence, and specifying an experiment whose result would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Engineer a self‐regenerative catalyst architecture by promoting in situ reversible exsolution of active metal nanoparticles from the multi‐principal‐element matrix during operation.
generation.material_initial_state: Near‐equiatomic multi‐principal‐element alloy catalyst with a uniform dispersion of metal elements.
generation.intervention: Incorporate design elements – such as minor dopants that introduce lattice strains and tailored heat treatment protocols – that enable controlled, reversible exsolution and reintegration of metal nanoparticles under cyclic oxidizing and reducing conditions.
generation.conditions: Simulated automotive exhaust conditions exhibiting dynamic redox cycling (alternating oxidizing and reducing environments), transient low-temperature operation (<150 °C), and high-temperature thermal aging (up to 800–900 °C) to accelerate durability testing.
generation.structural_mediator: Reversible formation and dissolution of nano‐sized metal clusters at the catalyst’s surface which effectively refresh active sites while suppressing irreversible sintering and poisoning by corrosive species.
generation.mechanism: During reducing episodes the host matrix exsolves finely dispersed metal clusters that deliver high catalytic activity; upon exposure to oxidizing conditions, these metal clusters reintegrate into the matrix, thereby preventing excessive particle growth and maintaining a robust active surface. This cyclic regeneration mitigates poisoning and retains catalytic performance over the long term.
generation.predicted_outcome: Sustained low‐temperature catalytic activity with improved resistance to CO, H2O, and NO poisoning and enhanced lifetime durability accompanied by minimal loss of platinum-group-metal utilization.
generation.baseline: The unmodified multi‐principal‐element catalyst initially exhibits good activity but gradually experiences sintering and irreversible active‐site loss under continuous operation without self‐regeneration.
generation.boundary: The self‐regenerative mechanism is contingent on sufficient and balanced redox cycling. If the exhaust conditions remain overly reducing or overly oxidizing, the reversible exsolution may be hindered, reducing the benefit.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative dynamics of the exsolution/reintegration rates and their net effect on long‐term performance under real-world automotive transient profiles remain to be precisely determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of catalysts: one engineered with the reversible exsolution mechanism via dopants and tailored heat treatments, and a control catalyst without these features. Subject both to alternating oxidizing/reducing cycles that mimic realistic automotive exhaust conditions alongside high-temperature aging.
measurements: In situ environmental TEM or XAFS to monitor nanoparticle exsolution/reintegration during cycling
Catalytic performance metrics, particularly T50 and full conversion temperatures over multiple cycles
Post-cycling particle size distribution using TEM/XRD
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the engineered catalyst does not display reversible exsolution/reintegration or if its long-term catalytic activity and poisoning resistance show no statistically significant improvement over the control, then the self‐regenerative hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: CO is an asphyxiating gas toxic to humans at concentrations exceeding 0.1%.[  ] The primary sources of CO emissions are motor vehicle exhaust and industrial flue gas, produced by the incomplete combustion of fossil fuels.[  ] Currently, the catalytic oxidation of CO is thought to be the most effective and energy‐efficient technique for purifying CO. The catalytic oxidation of CO is a key heterogeneous gas‐solid process and a valuable probe for studying catalyst structure, metal‒support interactions, adsorption‐desorption behavior, and reaction mechanisms.[  ] The catalytic activity, stability, and water tolerance of the Pt/HEO for CO oxidation were systematically evaluated. As shown in Figure 4a, the Pt/HEO catalyst achieved full CO conversion at 195 °C, significantly lower than the 430 °C required by HEO nanofibers alone (Figure S33, Supporting Information), highlighting the critical role of Pt nanoparticles. Interestingly, the catalytic performance of the Pt/HEO improved substantially after thermal aging. After aging in N2 at 700 °C, the conversion temperature dropped to 182 °C. AbstractThe sintering of Supported Transition Metal Catalysts (STMCs) is a core issue during high temperature catalysis. Perovskite oxides as host matrix for STMCs are proven to be sintering-resistance, leading to a family of self-regenerative materials. However, none other design principles for self-regenerative catalysts were put forward since 2002, which cannot satisfy diverse catalytic processes. Herein, inspired by the principle of high entropy-stabilized structure, a concept whether entropy driving force could promote the self-regeneration process is proposed. To verify it, a high entropy cubic Zr0.5(NiFeCuMnCo)0.5Ox is constructed as a host model, and interestingly in situ reversible exsolution-dissolution of supported metallic species are observed in multi redox cycles. Notably, in situ exsolved transition metals from high entropy Zr0.5(NiFeCuMnCo)0.5Ox support, whose entropic contribution (TΔSconfig = T⋆12.7 J mol−1 K−1) is predominant in ∆G, affording ultrahigh thermal stability in long-term CO2 hydrogenation (400 °C, >500 h).
